findings.reason: The protected solution is concise, conventional, and interview-ready. The names left, right, and middle clearly express the half-open lower-bound search interval and its probe. The final bound and equality checks are direct, and there is no exact generic local named index.

For distinct ascending integers, advancing d positions increases the array value by at least d, so arr[i] - i is non-decreasing. The half-open binary search maintains that every position before left has arr[position] < position and searches for the first position where arr[position] >= position. A probe below its position cannot be a fixed point and neither can any earlier position, so left advances; otherwise the probe remains a possible first boundary. At termination, equality returns the smallest fixed point. A boundary beyond the array or a strictly positive difference proves no later equality can exist, so -1 is correct.

Metadata consistently identifies Premium LeetCode problem 1064, Python, and the native fixedPoint(arr) interface. Authenticated source evidence confirms 1 through 9999 distinct integers in ascending order with values from -10^9 through 10^9. The app-local solve adapter preserves zero-based index equality, smallest-index selection when several fixed points exist, the -1 impossible-result sentinel, and the integer return contract.

The protected app source and immutable native source bound to verified submission 2067470816 are algorithmically identical: both use the same half-open interval [0, len(arr)), move left only when arr[middle] < middle, otherwise retain middle in the right half-boundary, and perform the same final in-range equality check before returning -1. Their only structural differences are the required Solution.fixedPoint wrapper and native typing syntax.

The three hidden workloads grow strictly ascending arrays from 128 through 8192 elements, a 64x span, and place the only fixed point at the final position, forcing a left-to-right scan to inspect every value while lower-bound search halves its interval. The exact protected source passed all eleven visible correctness cases and all three performance tiers with relative growth exponent +0.00 and a 1.00x largest runtime ratio. An independently correct linear scan matched every correctness and benchmark output but failed only the calibrated complexity verdict at +0.78 and 43.61x, distinguishing O(log N) binary search from O(N) scanning.

The Approach accurately derives monotonicity of arr[i] - i from distinct ascending integers, formulates the first arr[i] >= i lower bound, explains why immediate equality return could miss an earlier fixed point, and justifies final verification. Its edge cases cover the first position, multiple matches, an exhausted interval, strictly positive candidate difference, and negative values. The O(log N) time and O(1) auxiliary-space claims match the protected implementation and branch manifest.

The modular Reference preserves distinct ascending input, zero-based fixed-point equality, minimum-index selection, the -1 fallback, all three explained source examples, both live constraints, the better-than-O(N) follow-up, and the source's linear-scan hint. The live statement contains no images, diagrams, tables, or notes.

The authenticated live Premium statement directly verified exactly three examples in source order with exact arrays, outputs, and explanations; distinct ascending input; smallest-index selection; two constraints; the better-than-O(N) follow-up; and one linear-scan hint. source_fidelity.json binds those facts and every composed local section to the reviewed statement hash abe8deb5bd8835a4aa4a79f33b117102f9da99ba8da7a8d772c519c28fd82adf.

coverage: The authenticated Premium statement contains exactly three examples. Their exact arrays and outputs appear first in source order, with explanations for the middle fixed point, the zero fixed point, and the absent result.
All eleven ordinary correctness cases are visible samples or trials. They cover length endpoints 1 and 9999, value endpoints -10^9 and 10^9, zero-based equality, and the -1 sentinel.

Material behavior includes a match at the first, middle, and final index; several fixed points requiring the smallest; single-element match and absence; every value below its index; every value above its index; and a boundary-spanning array with no match.

An independent left-to-right oracle returns the first position whose value equals its index and otherwise returns -1. It recomputed every authored expected value without using monotonicity, lower bounds, or binary search.

The oracle, protected app source, and immutable native Solution agreed on all 14 authored correctness-plus-benchmark inputs, 12910 exhaustive distinct ascending arrays drawn from -5 through 8 up to length eight, 5000 deterministic random legal arrays up to length 200, and eight explicit boundary arrays. The authored maximum-length case independently exercises all 9999 legal positions.

The 128-, 1024-, and 8192-element late-match workloads remain hidden and performance-only, use size consistently as N, and span 64x. A correct O(N) scan matched every output and failed only scaling at +0.78 and 43.61x, while the O(log N) protected source passed at +0.00 and 1.00x.
